Quick Recap - Linear Regression

  • Assume we have input \(X = (X_1,\ldots,X_n)\) and output \(Y = (Y_1,\ldots,Y_n)\) (example: \(X_i\) is month index, \(Y_i\) is demand for product A)

  • We assume that the “true” demand is \(f(X_i) = \alpha + \beta X_i\)

  • The “observed” demand is a noisy version of the “true” demand: \(\alpha + \beta X_i + \epsilon_i\)

\[\begin{align} \widehat \beta = \displaystyle\frac{\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \bar X)(Y_i - \bar Y)}{\sum_{i=1}^n(X_i - \bar X)^2}, & & \widehat \alpha = \bar Y - \widehat\beta \bar X. \end{align}\]

Model Checking for Linear Regression

  • Linear regression relies on some basic assumptions, that underlie the theory behind this model

  • Assumes the true model we saw 1 slide ago

  • Can we check those assumptions?

    • Yes, but not in this class (Stat 302/305)
    • We will focus on comparing this model using prediction

Back to original example

library(RSQLite)
db <- dbConnect(SQLite(), dbname = "xcoretail.sqlite")
dbListTables(db)
[1] "prices" "sales" 
library(DBI)
months <- sprintf("2011-%02d", 1:12)
counts <- rep(NA, 12)
for(i in 1:length(counts)) {
  query <- sqlInterpolate(db, "SELECT SUM(Quantity) FROM sales
                        WHERE StockCode = '71053' AND
                        InvoiceDate LIKE ?month",
  month = paste0(months[i], "%") )
  request <- dbSendQuery(db, query)
  counts[i] <- as.numeric(dbFetch(request))
  dbClearResult(request)
}
plot(x = 1:12, y = counts, xlab = "Months", ylab = "Total Sales")

Predicting the next month

  • Suppose it’s October 1st and we want to predict how many sales there will be in the month

  • Can we do this using linear regression?

    • Yes

  • How do we decide if our model is any good?

    • Compare it to the true number of sales

Prediction

  • Lets fit a linear regression to the first 9 months
x <- 1:9
y <- counts[1:9]

fit <- lm(y ~ x)
fit

Call:
lm(formula = y ~ x)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)            x  
     107.44        10.93

Prediction

  • This gives us a fitted model

\[ \widehat{f}(X_i) = \widehat{\alpha} + \widehat{\beta}X_i \]

  • We could just evaluate this when \(X_i=10\) for the next month

\[ \widehat{f}(X_i = 10) = 107.44 + 10.93 \times 10 = 216.74 \]

  • Is this a good prediction?

Measuring Prediction

  • We could compare the estimate to the true value, in terms of squared difference, a similar quantity to that used to fit the regression model initially

  • For new data \(x_{new},y_{new}\), which was not used to fit the model, compute

\[ \text{Prediction Error} = (y_{new} - \widehat{f}(x_{new}))^2 \]

\[ \text{Prediction Error} = (y_{new} - \widehat{f}(x_{new}))^2 \]

  • For this problem
alpha_hat <- as.numeric(coef(fit)[1])
beta_hat <- as.numeric(coef(fit)[2])
alpha_hat
[1] 107.4444
beta_hat
[1] 10.93333
y_hat <- alpha_hat + beta_hat * 10
Error <- (y_hat - counts[10])^2
Error
[1] 20672.05
  • This is just a number, can’t do anything with just a single number

Evaluating Predictions

  • Come back to this after (very briefly) introducing an alternative method for doing prediction

K-Nearest Neighbours

Other prediction methods

  • We have seen one initial method for predicting a numeric quantity, linear regression

  • This is a simple but essential data science method

  • We will now see another key method, which is quite different

A Quick Note

  • For the previous example, we wanted to predict the sales for the next month only, when \(x_{new} = x + 1\)

  • This is kind of a special case, we want our method to be able to predict at any value of \(x\) normally

  • We will see this in our next example and in all future examples

House Price Data

  • Here we will use data about the sale price of ~1000 houses sold in California in 2008
house_sales <- read.csv("house_prices.csv")
plot(x = house_sales$area, y = house_sales$price, xlab = "Area (Sq ft)",
     ylab = "Sale Price")

A Different Prediction Approach

  • Suppose we want to predict the sale price of a new house (not in this dataset) which has an area of 2500 sq ft?

  • We could do this with regression, find the value of \(\widehat{\alpha} +\widehat{\beta}\times 2500\)

  • This requires the assumptions of a linear regression

  • Instead, lets do something very simple

Neighbors

  • Find the 10 rows in our dataset with \(x\) value “closest” to the one we want to predict at

  • Get the average of \(Y\) for these 10 rows

  • Use that as the prediction for a new house with \(X=2500\)

What this looks like

Notes

  • How do we decide what points are closest?

  • Squared distance, \((X - 2500)^2\)

  • Would this work if we had instead chosen the 3 nearest points?

  • End up with a very similar estimate (for this example)

K-Nearest Neighbours

  • This is the K in the name!

  • How many neighbours do we use in our model?

  • What is the right value of \(K\) for this problem?

  • The solution to this is the same as the one needed to compare our linear regression model from before

Comparing Prediction Methods

Fitting a Model to Data

  • Think back to how we fit linear regression

    • We find the model which minimizes the sum of squared errors on our data!

  • This gives us the best possible regression model for our data

  • But we want to see if its the best model for new/different data

  • Several ways to do this

Training and Test Data

  • Suppose we were trying to see how good our regression model is at predicting house prices here

  • If this is all the data we have, we need to find a way to get “new” data

  • The way to do this is to split our dataset into:

    • A training set
    • A test set

  • Estimate our model using the training data

  • See how good it does at predicting the test data

    • Because we didn’t use the test data for fitting the model, this is predicting on new data

  • This is the standard way to evaluate models used for prediction

  • We just need some metric for performance on the test data

Test Data

  • The test data has to be “new” data

  • Data that was not used to estimate the model initially

  • Otherwise we are cheating, won’t really tell us how good the model is at predicting

    • Known as overfitting

The Exact Procedure for Linear Regression

  • We have data \((X_i, Y_i)\)

  • We randomly put 70% of this data in the training set and 30% in the test set (the proportions can vary)

  • We estimate \(\widehat{\alpha}\) and \(\widehat{\beta}\) using only the training data

  • We see how good the model is at predicting \(Y\) in the test data

What this looks like

Measuring Performance

  • We need a measure of “performance” on the test data

  • For a single point earlier we considered

\[ \text{Prediction Error} = (y_{new} - \widehat{f}(x_{new}))^2 \]

  • We need something like this, for all data in the test set

  • Average it across the data in the test set

RMSPE

For \((X_i^{test},Y_{i}^{test})\) in the test set we will compute

\[ RSMPE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{test}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{test}}(Y_{i}^{test} - \widehat{f}(X_{i}^{test}))^2} \]

  • Here \(\widehat{\alpha}\) and \(\widehat{\beta}\) are computed from the training data!

  • Then \(\widehat{f}(X_{i}^{test})= \widehat{\alpha}+\widehat{\beta}X_{i}^{test} = \widehat{Y}_i^{test}\)

  • The point on the fitted line, for the \(X\) in the test set

  • This is the Root Mean Squared Predicted Error

Computing this

  • Let’s split this house price data into a training and test split and compute the RMSPE
set.seed(240)
prop_train <- 0.7
prop_test <- 1 - prop_train

n_data <- nrow(house_sales)

train_test <- sample(c("Train", "Test"),
                     size = n_data, replace = TRUE, 
                     prob = c(prop_train, prop_test))
head(train_test)
[1] "Train" "Test"  "Train" "Train" "Train" "Train"
head(train_test == "Train")
[1]  TRUE FALSE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE  TRUE

Splitting the data

train_data <- house_sales[train_test == "Train", ]
test_data <- house_sales[train_test == "Test",]

nrow(train_data)/n_data
[1] 0.7149877
nrow(test_data)/n_data
[1] 0.2850123
  • train_test a vector indicating which rows are in which, then we subset using this to separate the data into the two subsets

Fit to Training Data

fit_train <- lm(price ~ area, data = train_data)
fit_train

Call:
lm(formula = price ~ area, data = train_data)

Coefficients:
(Intercept)         area  
    30894.1        124.7
  • These estimates will change if we have a different training set

Exercise

  • Rerun the code to create the training and test sets, using a different seed (which will lead to a different sample). Confirm the estimates of \(\alpha\) and \(\beta\) change when you do.

Solution

Getting Predictions

  • Now we need to get predictions for \(Y\) for our test data

  • We can use the R function predict to do this

est_Y <- predict(fit_train, newdata = test_data)
head(est_Y)
       2       13       14       16       19       21 
176446.0 139527.9 158111.7 172330.1 104231.3 170334.5

  • These are our estimates of \(\widehat{Y}_{i}^{test}\)

  • predict fits the model fit_train, using the \(X\) values from test_data (i.e, it knows \(X\) is area)

Computing RMSPE

  • We need to compute \[ RMSPE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{test}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{test}}(Y_{i}^{test} - \widehat{f}(X_{i}^{test}))^2} \]

  • This is the same as

\[ RMSPE = \sqrt{\frac{1}{n_{test}}\sum_{i=1}^{n_{test}}(Y_{i}^{test} - \widehat{Y}_{i}^{test})^2} \]

  • We just computed est_Y and can get \(Y_{i}^{test}\) from test_data$price
RMSPE <- sqrt( mean( (est_Y - test_data$price) ^2) )
RMSPE
[1] 76317.91
  • We have no other model to compare this to, can’t really say if it’s good or bad

Fitting KNN

  • We will briefly fit KNN to this data next with \(K=5\)

  • We’ll spend more time on this next week, but for now will just see how to do it

library(caret)

fit_knn <- knnreg(price ~ area, data = train_data, k = 5)
est_Y_knn <- predict(fit_knn, test_data)
head(est_Y_knn)
[1] 135550.0 103313.2 144102.8 144098.0 103723.7 152950.0

Compute RMSPE

RMSPE_knn <- sqrt( mean( (est_Y_knn - test_data$price) ^2) )
RMSPE_knn
[1] 82518.13

  • This is larger than the RMSPE for linear regression, indicates that linear regression can better predict house prices using the area, for this data

  • Compared to KNN with \(K=5\). But why \(K=5\)?

Exercise

  • Refit KNN with \(K=10\)

  • What is the RMSPE for this model on the test data?
